title: Rumi's quatrains
hook: many four-line poems carry Rumi's name, some by others
tomorrow: what did Rumi tell his son on the night he was dying?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a quatrain that isn't Rumi's, and its real home: come back, the turning called tawba. Right name, please. So which four-line poems are his?
screen: `RIGHT NAME, PLEASE.` → `WHICH FOUR LINES ARE HIS?`

segments.voice: Zoe has written four lines for the memorial card, and Inés's aunt says poems are too fancy for grief. Rumi might half agree. In his table talk, the Discourses, he says he has no taste for poetry. He speaks it because the people who come to him want it, the way a host washes out tripe because his guest has an appetite for tripe. And yet his collected poems hold a large set of quatrains.
screen: `TOO FANCY FOR GRIEF?` → `NO TASTE FOR POETRY.` → `TRIPE FOR A GUEST.`

segments.voice: A rubai is a Persian four-line poem, with the first, second and fourth lines rhyming, built for one sharp thought. Here's the catch: quatrains travel. Short and easy to remember, they get passed around, and some that carry Rumi's name also turn up under other poets' names. So his editors sort them with care. Now the debate, inside his own tradition, about what the poems are for. One view takes Rumi at his word. The poetry is the side dish; the meal is the path itself, the Quran, prayer, the company of the friend. Its best case: a teacher who says don't fall for my rhymes is protecting you from loving the wrapping instead of the gift. The other view hears a host's modesty. His son Sultan Walad and the Mevlevi order that grew from his circle kept the poems, sang them, and built their gatherings around them. For Sufis, sama, listening to poetry and music, can be a road toward God. Its best case: if the guests are hungry and only this dish will feed them, the dish is the hospitality. Both sides agree on one thing. The four lines are served to someone.
screen: `RUBAI: FOUR LINES, ONE THOUGHT.` · `QUATRAINS TRAVEL BETWEEN NAMES.` · `ONE VIEW: THE POEM IS THE SIDE DISH.` · `THE OTHER: SAMA, A ROAD TO GOD.` · then, large: `FOUR LINES, FOR A GUEST.`

segments.voice: Write four short lines by hand for someone who's grieving or tired, rhyming the first, second and fourth if the rhymes come easily. Keep it plain; a dish made for a guest is still a meal. At the end, read it once and change one word.
Rubai: a Persian four-line poem, lines one, two and four rhyming. Short enough to remember, and to wander off under the wrong name.
Keep this one: four lines, served to a guest who is hungry for them. Five days with Rumi again, and the next one is hard.

screen: `DAY 1501 COUNTS.` → `RUMI AGAIN · 5 OF 8.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DID RUMI TELL HIS SON THE NIGHT HE WAS DYING?`

howItsDone: Readers of Persian know the rubai as a short form for a single thought; Rumi's quatrains are printed in editions of his Divan, and Mevlevi gatherings sing his poems with music during the sama.

fork.setup: at a Mevlevi gathering, a newcomer quotes the tripe line: 'so the poems don't matter.' what's the other side's best case?

fork.reveal: a host's modesty doesn't make the meal nothing. the Mevlevis kept and sang the poems; for them, sama can be a road toward God.

chat.says: wrote 4 lines for the memorial card. ines's aunt says poems are too fancy for grief. is she right?
options: Even Rumi called verse a dish for guests. Keep it plain; the card's for them.
She's right. Rumi himself said poetry is worthless, so skip the poem.
Make it longer. A real Rumi rubai runs eight lines or more.
chat.meaning: In his Discourses Rumi says he serves poetry the way a host serves a dish the guests want. Four plain lines for grieving guests fit.
